stories.headline: India Inc bullish on growth story: KM Birla
stories.title: India Inc bullish on growth story: KM Birla
stories.summary: India Inc.'s conviction in the country's growth prospects is possibly the highest in a long time and capital discipline is being mistaken for lack of commitment toward expanding capacities, said Kumar Mangalam Birla, chairman, Aditya Birla Group, at The Economic Times World Leaders Forum.There is enough capacity buildout happening on the ground with new plants springing up across the country and bank loan numbers pointing to robust economic activity, said the chief of the cement to consumer conglomerate valued at more than $118 billion. "I don't think we should confuse capital discipline with conviction about India,'' Birla said in a fireside chat with ET's Sruthijith KK. "Advances to corporates from banks have gone up by 20% compared to last year... and that is pretty evenly spread between small and medium enterprises as well." While the macro economy has been growing at the fastest pace among major peers, Indian industry is being blamed for not being aggressive in expanding capacities as new plants are coming up slower than in the past. Companies which binged on debt in the past cycles have been deleveraging and are a lot more cautious in expanding capacities to avoid repeating past mistakes. Birla, whose group itself has lined up $30 billion to expand capacities, said investment decisions are taken considering several factors including returns, volatility, industry needs and global events. "It is more of a capital discipline exercise,'' he said.ALSO READ | India Inc’s got all it takes to roll out ‘World+1’ model, says KM BirlaIn the last few years, the Aditya Birla Group has grown across most of its businesses amid a pandemic, wars, interest rate hikes, tariffs and energy shocks. The global economy seems to have grown "shock absorbers" in this period, and individual economies as well as corporations are learning to deal with a lot more stress, Birla said. "There are no more perma-friends or perma-enemies. There are only perma-issues," he said. The diversified conglomerate has taken a contrarian view in this period to grow across its traditional as well as new growth platforms. "It's been a two-part strategy," Birla said. For its overseas businesses, the group wants to be a "multi-local," setting up manufacturing plants close to consumers. "So, we have the supply chain flexibility and are not impacted by tariff wars or geopolitical bigotries," he said.ALSO READ | ET WLF 2026: Private players discuss India’s path from defence importer to global powerHindalco Industries' integrated aluminium plant being set up at Bay Minette in North America for a capital expenditure of $5 billion, for instance, is meant to primarily cater to customers in North America, Birla said.The growth in businesses in India, meanwhile, is reflecting the country's economy and its story, he said. "You need a strong economy to produce strong businesses. People talk about China+1 for India, and whilst that's a convenient shorthand, it's intellectually very lazy," Birla said. The narrative for India should now move to World+1, given that India has the capabilities and track record, and can be a "growth engine" for the world, he said.Lack of ease in doing business is not unique to India and almost every country and region has its own issues, he said, citing an example of how in an advanced economy one of his companies had to shift the plant's location due to environmental issues after working on it for months. "We are not the only people who have issues like land, environment, judicial, local laws etc," he said.The Aditya Birla Group is the largest producer of cement, refined copper, cellulosic fibre in the country besides housing the largest branded and lifestyle entity. It is also one of the largest producers of aluminium domestically, and a dominant player in paints, telecom and non-banking financial services. Several of its businesses are seeing high competitive intensity. "An important part of running a business is to compete and compete well. And risk-taking is an important part too, or you might as well not be in business," he said. While it is good to have a "rear view" of competition, the group focuses on doing what it does best-running plants and investing deeply in its ecosystems, he said. "We have very deep customer relationships. We have increased capacity exponentially. When you have been in industries for a long time, there is an accumulated knowledge that you have the advantage of," he said.Birla said the telecom business, which has been challenging for years, has turned the corner and it would be a credible and a profitable "number three" player as it invests in 4G and 5G.Novelis, its North American aluminium business, has stabilised after a fire accident and is ramping up. Plans to list are off the table as the company hasn't been getting the valuation that it hoped for. "We have no compulsion to do an IPO. There is no need for us to raise funds, so I don't see that happening now at all," he said.The world's largest producer of flat-rolled aluminium products, Novelis was to have listed in the US in 2024. "We put back the plans at that time because we were not getting the kind of value discovery that we thought or hoped we would or we were told we would. There was no other reason to want to list," Birla said.Hindalco's focus would now be to commission and ramp up the plant at Bay Minette, which will be pivotal for the company's future, he said.

stories.headline: Stray Dog Crisis and the Control Measures
stories.title: Stray Dog Crisis and the Control Measures
stories.summary: Every morning, as dawn breaks over the lanes of Jammu and Kashmir, a quiet emergency unfolds. Children tighten their grip on their schoolbags, elderly residents mentally map their routes to avoid known dog packs, and shopkeepers hesitate before unlocking their shutters, scanning the street for any sign of a lurking threat. These are not irrational fears; they are daily survival tactics in a region where, on average, every ten minutes, another person is bitten by a dog. This is the arithmetic of official government data, and it reveals a public health crisis of staggering proportions—one that demands the immediate attention of every parent, policymaker, and medical professional in Jammu and Kashmir. The numbers are not just alarming; they are accelerating at a terrifying pace. Between 2022 and 2025, the Union Territory recorded over 2.12 lakh dog bite cases, but the trajectory tells the real story. Cases surged from 22,110 in 2022 to 34,664 in 2023, then jumped to 51,027 in 2024, and crossed 55,312 in 2025. Jammu and Kashmir now records 425 dog bites per 100,000 people annually—nearly three times the rate reported in Delhi. That translates to an average of 150 people being bitten every single day. With 23 stray dogs for every 1,000 people, J&K holds the second-highest stray dog density in the country. How did we arrive at this precipice? The answer lies not in inevitability but in three interconnected failures, all rooted in choices we have consistently refused to make. The first and most fundamental driver is waste management. Open garbage dumps have become the primary engine of stray dog population growth. Wherever food is freely available, dogs congregate, breed exponentially, and survive. Rapid urbanization has created vast, unregulated waste accumulation sites that act as permanent feeding grounds for feral populations. Without addressing this infrastructure collapse, no population control programme can succeed. The second failure is the systemic neglect of the Animal Birth Control programme. India's ABC Rules, mandated by law and endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO), require municipal bodies to systematically sterilize and vaccinate stray dogs through a Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (CNVR) approach. Yet, between June 2023 and September 2025, J&K managed to sterilize and vaccinate just 48,998 stray dogs against an estimated population of over 1.5 lakh—a fraction of what is needed even to halt growth, let alone reverse it. More revealing still: official data placed before the Legislative Assembly confirmed that only 935 dogs were sterilized in Srinagar in the entire year of 2025. In many districts, the ABC programme has collapsed before it ever meaningfully began, stalled by administrative delays, expired contracts, and slow tendering processes. The third failure occurs after a bite has already occurred, when the post-exposure prophylaxis — the vaccine course that stands between a dog bite and a rabies fatality, is often initiated days or weeks later, if it is sought at all. This delay turns a preventable tragedy into an inevitable fatality. The solution to this crisis is not a mystery, nor does it require unattainable technology. The WHO specifies that vaccinating at least 70% of a dog population is sufficient to interrupt rabies transmission, but achieving that threshold requires a permanent, adequately funded, and monitored ward-level programme, not just sporadic campaigns. In a landmark judgment on May 19, 2026, the Supreme Court reinforced the ABC Rules 2023, directing that all schools, hospitals, bus stands, and public complexes must be securely fenced to prevent stray entry, while mandating regular pick-up drives and mandatory sterilization. Yet, court orders alone cannot save lives; implementation on the ground will. We must radically overhaul our solid waste management—enclosed bins, regular collection, and the outright elimination of open dump sites must accompany sterilization efforts. Simultaneously, every district hospital must have a functional anti-rabies clinic with an uninterrupted vaccine supply and staff trained in proper wound management. Public education must be treated as a clinical intervention in itself: persistent, delivered in local languages, reaching every village through health workers, schools, panchayats, and local media. We possess the scientific knowledge, the legal framework, and the resources to bring this crisis under control. What we lack is the collective will to act decisively and consistently. (The author is a Veterinarian and an Independent Researcher. Email: dr.akhterrasool@rediffmail.com)
